summary: Senegal lies at the westernmost tip of Africa and became independent from France in 1960; it is politically relatively stable and known for its Sufi brotherhoods, its music and its culture of hospitality, 'teranga'.

ranking.name: Islam (Sunni)
ranking.description: Islam reached the Senegal River valley in the 11th century through trans-Saharan trade, and around 1040 the ruler of the Kingdom of Takrur became one of the first monarchs in West Africa to convert to Islam. But Islam truly took root among the people during French colonial rule in the late 19th century, when the Sufi brotherhoods became central to resistance to colonialism and to social reorganization: in 1883 Amadou Bamba founded the Mouride order, and the Tijaniyya, Qadiriyya and other orders also expanded rapidly. Today almost all Senegalese Muslims belong to a Sufi order, and every year millions of followers travel to Touba for the Grand Magal pilgrimage.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Catholicism was briefly introduced when the Portuguese arrived in the 15th century, and developed in cities such as Saint-Louis, Gorée Island and Dakar during French colonial rule in the 19th century. Catholics are mainly the Jola of Casamance in the south and the Serer of the west, as well as the mixed-race communities of the cities. Senegal's first president, Senghor, was a Catholic who nonetheless governed a predominantly Muslim country for twenty years, which embodies the tradition of religious tolerance.

ranking.name: Traditional beliefs
ranking.description: Before Islam and Christianity became widespread, each of Senegal's peoples had its own traditional beliefs; for example, the Serer worshipped the supreme god Roog. Because Islamization and Christianization are more than a hundred years old, few people now follow purely traditional religion, mainly in the southeast and parts of Casamance, but many traditional customs have been incorporated into Islamic practice.

religion.background: Senegal came into contact with Islam in the 11th century, but it was not until French colonial rule in the 19th century that the Sufi brotherhoods made Islam widespread among the people, and the Mouride, Tijaniyya and other orders still have far-reaching influence in society and politics today. Catholicism developed in cities and in the south with French colonization. After independence in 1960 Senegal became a secular state, and the tradition of Muslims and Christians living together in peace and intermarrying has made it regarded as a model of religious tolerance in West Africa.

language.official: French is the official language, and several indigenous languages, including Wolof, are national languages.

ranking.name: Wolof
ranking.description: Wolof belongs to the Atlantic branch of the Niger–Congo family and was the language of the Wolof Empire of the 14th to 16th centuries. During the colonial period cities such as Dakar and Saint-Louis were dominated by the Wolof, and urbanization made Wolof the common language among the various groups, so that about forty percent of the population speak it as their mother tongue and more than eighty percent can speak Wolof. In cities, 'Urban Wolof', mixed with French vocabulary, is common.

ranking.name: Fula (Pulaar)
ranking.description: Fula (Pulaar) is the language of the Fulani and the Toucouleur, spoken in the northern Senegal River valley and in the east. The Fulani are known for pastoral nomadism and Islamic scholarship, and both the Kingdom of Takrur in the 11th century and the Islamic state of Futa Toro in the 18th and 19th centuries had Pulaar as their main language.

ranking.name: Jola
ranking.description: Jola is the language of the Jola people of the southern Casamance region. Casamance is separated from the rest of the north by The Gambia, and its culture differs considerably from the north; the Casamance separatist movement since 1982 is related to this regional identity.

ranking.name: French
ranking.description: French has been the official language since independence in 1960, stemming from French colonial rule; Saint-Louis became France's base in West Africa as early as 1659. French is used in government, education and formal occasions, but only about 2% speak French as a mother tongue, and most people use Wolof for daily communication.

language.history: Senegal has more than thirty indigenous languages, and after Islamization some were written in an adapted Arabic script called 'Ajami'. From the 17th century France established bases at Saint-Louis and Gorée Island, and after the 19th century French became the language of colonial administration and education. After independence in 1960 the first president, Senghor, a famous French-language poet, kept French as the official language. From 1971 the government successively designated Wolof, Pulaar, Jola, Serer and other languages as national languages.

ranking.name: Thieboudienne (fish and rice)
ranking.description: Fresh fish such as grouper is stewed in a tomato sauce with vegetables such as cassava, carrots, eggplant and cabbage, and then broken rice is cooked in the stewing broth, so that the rice absorbs the fish's flavor; the crispy crust at the bottom of the pot is especially prized.
ranking.history: Thieboudienne is said to have been invented in the 19th century by the Saint-Louis cook Penda Mbaye, who used broken rice in place of the traditional millet. During the French colonial period large quantities of broken rice were imported from Indochina, so that rice replaced millet as Senegal's staple. In 2021 UNESCO inscribed thieboudienne on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity; it is regarded as Senegal's national dish, and its name in Wolof means 'rice and fish'.

ranking.name: Chicken yassa
ranking.description: Chicken or fish is marinated in plenty of onions, lemon juice, mustard and spices, then grilled and stewed together with the marinade's onions, giving a tangy, slightly spicy flavor, eaten with rice.
ranking.history: Yassa originated with the Jola people of the southern Casamance region, where limes and lemons are abundant. The dish spread across the country with internal migration and exchange within Senegal, and to other West African countries and France. Because it is simple to make and the ingredients are easy to obtain, chicken yassa is a common dish for everyday family meals and for entertaining guests, and it is also one of the most popular dishes of Senegalese restaurants abroad.

ranking.name: Mafé (peanut stew)
ranking.description: Beef, lamb or chicken is stewed with tomato, onion, sweet potato and cassava in a large amount of peanut butter into a thick sauce, with a rich flavor, and eaten with white rice.
ranking.history: Peanuts originated in the Americas and were introduced to West Africa by the Portuguese in the 16th century. In the 19th century the French colonial authorities strongly promoted peanut cultivation in Senegal as an export crop, and Senegal was for a time one of the world's largest peanut exporters, with railways built along the peanut-growing areas. Mafé originated with the Mandinka of Mali and became an everyday dish in Senegal under the impetus of the peanut industry.

ranking.name: Thiakry (millet and yogurt dessert)
ranking.description: Steamed millet grains are mixed with yogurt or fermented milk, sugar, vanilla and nutmeg, sometimes with raisins added, giving a sweet-sour, refreshing texture.
ranking.history: Millet is one of the oldest grains in West Africa and was Senegal's staple before rice became widespread. Thiakry combines millet with the dairy products of the nomadic Fulani, reflecting the exchange relationship between farmers and herders. It is a common dessert for breaking the fast during Ramadan and at festivals, and is also a popular chilled snack in hot weather.

ranking.name: Akara (bean fritters)
ranking.description: Peeled black-eyed peas are soaked and ground into a puree, mixed with onion and salt, scooped with a spoon into small balls and deep-fried, crisp outside and soft inside, often dipped in a sauce of onion, tomato and chili.
ranking.history: Akara derives from the Yoruba 'akara' of Nigeria; black-eyed peas are a native West African crop, and similar bean fritters exist throughout West Africa. It also traveled to Brazil with the slave trade and became the 'acarajé' of Bahia state. In Senegal, akara is a popular snack sold by street vendors in the evening, and is also often distributed to guests at naming ceremonies and religious festivals.
